newsitem.title: INDIA: India cyclone rescue work moves into full swing.
newsitem.headline: India cyclone rescue work moves into full swing.

text.p: Relief workers combed hundreds of flooded coastal villages on Saturday for survivors in India's cyclone-hit Andhra Pradesh state as fears mounted that the storm may have killed more than 1,000 people.
Two days after torrential rain and tidal waves surged up to five kms (three miles) inland, almost 40 or 50 villages were still marooned in the southeastern state, official sources said.
They said more than 800 villages, home to an estimated 2.5 million fishermen and farmers in an area known as the ricebowl of the state, were devastated by the fury of the cyclone.

"I am at a loss for words to describe the tragedy in which about 1,000 people may have lost their lives," Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister V. Chandrababu Naidu was quoted as saying by the Press Trust of India news agency.

Police and troops struggled through swirling floodwaters up to three metres (10 feet) deep to reach many isolated coastal villages. Six military helicopters flew continuous sorties to drop food and drinking water to the stranded, officials said.
"We are in the thick of cyclone work here," said R.V. Chandravadan, a magistrate in Rajahmundry town, supervising rescue efforts at the heart of the devastation. "I don't have time to talk."

Relief officials put the death toll at 477 late on Friday but expected it to rise. The local Eenadu newspaper put the toll at 671, saying that the bulk of the deaths were in the East Godavari district, where 570 people died.

The newspaper also reported more than 1,000 fishermen were missing. Officials said establishing accurate figures will be difficult as whole villages had been wiped out and tidal waters had scattered bodies.
Few houses survived the combination of flood waters and winds gusting at more than 180 km per hour (110 mph).
"About 225,000 homes have been completely razed by the storm," a government official told Reuters. "There has been nearly a million hectares of crop damaged."

About 615,000 hectares (1.5 million acres) of rice crops were destroyed, H.S. Brahma, who is heading the relief operation, said. An additional 312,000 hectares (770,640 acres) of bananas, coconuts and sugarcane were devastated.
Earlier, state government spokesman Nageswara Rao put the number of homes destroyed or damaged in the deluge at 400,000.

Television pictures showed people wading waist deep through flood waters, overturned trucks, cars, uprooted trees strewn across roads and bodies trapped beneath trees which had crashed on to their fragile houses. Aerial shots showed large expanses of land under water.
The United News of India agency said seven people had been admitted to hospital with symptoms similar to cholera, as health workers faced a possible epidemic.

"There is no scare of an epidemic so far, medical teams are functioning well. However, power supply at many ares is still disrupted to a large extent," Varanasi Suryanarayana, a resident of the area, told Reuters by telephone.
Relief officials said that more than 400 teams of doctors and paramedics had spread out to innoculate villagers and spray disinfectant and insecticides to combat disease.

Around 3.5 million people live in the fertile Konaseema region around the Godavari river delta. Andhra Pradesh's flat low-lying coastline leaves it vulnerable to tropical storms coming off the Bay of Bengal.

In 1977, more than 10,000 people were killed by a cyclone that drove a tidal wave up to 12 km (eight miles) inland. A cyclone killed 120 people in June this year, and 967 people died in another in 1990.
